summary: In Greek mythology, Canthus (Ancient Greek Κάνθος) is an Argonaut from Euboea — son of Canethus and grandson of Abas (or son of Abas). On the return from Colchis he is killed in Libya by Caphaurus (Cephalion) while raiding flocks; Valerius Flaccus alternatively has him fall to Gesander in the Colchian war.
etymology: Greek Κάνθος; Apollonius and Hyginus place him in the Argonaut catalogue from Euboea.

sections.heading: Argonaut slain in Libya
paragraphs: Apollonius Rhodius lists Canthus son of Canethus (Argonautica 1.77–85) and narrates his death in book 4: stranded in Libya, he pursues stolen sheep and is killed by Caphaurus son of Amphithemis and Tritonis; the Argonauts avenge him. Hyginus (Fabulae 14) and Valerius Flaccus repeat the Euboean Argonaut; Valerius also has a Colchian-war death at Gesander's hands.
Hyginus separately knows a Canthus son of Aegyptus slain by a Danaid Eurydice — a different figure, not this Argonaut node.

sections.heading: Homonym care
paragraphs: The atlas id canthus is the Argonaut alone — not the anatomical canthus (eye-corner), nor the Aegyptiad bridegroom of Hyginus Fabulae 170.
